description: Machine-readable guide to which chart in @headless-charts/react suits which question and data shape.
globalRules: `id` is required on every chart and must be unique in the document — it is the DOM id D3 selects on. Two charts sharing an id will render into the same node.

Charts read their size from the rendered element. Size them with `className` or `style` (e.g. `className="w-full h-64"`); there are no `width` or `height` props. A container with no height renders an empty chart.
Styling is headless: pass Tailwind (or any CSS) classes via `className` on the chart and via `className` on each series config. Nothing is coloured by default.
Use `margin` for space outside the plot area (axis labels live here) and `padding` for space inside it.
Tooltips are opt-in: pass `tooltip={{}}` for defaults, `tooltip={{ keys: [...] }}` to choose fields, or `tooltip={{ html: (d) => string }}` to take over rendering.
Animation is opt-in via `drawing={{ duration, delay }}`; charts render instantly by default.
Axis keys support dot paths into nested objects (e.g. `{ key: "user.score" }`).

decisionTree.question: How does a measure compare across named categories?

options.name: ColumnChart
options.when: Up to ~12 categories with short labels — vertical bars, grouped when several measures are passed

options.name: BarChart
options.when: Long category labels, or more than ~12 categories — horizontal bars give labels room

options.name: LollipopVChart
options.when: Values matter more than magnitude-as-area, and bars would look heavy; vertical orientation

options.name: LollipopHChart
options.when: Same as LollipopVChart but with long category labels

options.name: SpineChart
options.when: Two opposing measures per category read outward from a shared centre axis, e.g. male/female

options.name: RadarChart
options.when: Five or more metrics compared across a handful of entities on one shared 0–max scale

decisionTree.question: What is this made of — how do parts add to a whole?

options.name: PieChart
options.when: One whole split into ~6 or fewer slices at a single point in time

options.name: ColumnChartStacked
options.when: Composition compared across several categories or periods, vertical

options.name: BarChartStacked
options.when: Same as ColumnChartStacked but with long category labels; also does waterfall

options.name: AreaChart
options.when: Composition changing over a continuous axis; supports 100% and streamgraph stacking

options.name: PizzaChart
options.when: Several metrics as radial segments of one entity, each against its own max

decisionTree.question: How does a measure change over time or an ordered axis?

options.name: LineChart
options.when: Trend of one or more series; the default choice for time on x

options.name: AreaChart
options.when: Trend where the volume under the line or the split of a total matters

options.name: ColumnChart
options.when: Few discrete periods where individual values matter more than the trend line

options.name: TimeLineChart
options.when: Discrete events or durations on a date axis rather than a continuous measure

decisionTree.question: How do two measures relate to each other?

options.name: ScatterPlot
options.when: One point per record; encodes up to two more categorical and one more numeric dimension via color, shape and size

options.name: WaffleChart
options.when: Both axes are categorical (or binned) and a third value is encoded as cell colour — a heatmap

decisionTree.question: How are the values of one measure spread out?

options.name: ColumnChart
options.when: Histogram of raw continuous values — set `x.bin` and bar heights become counts

options.name: BarChart
options.when: Same histogram horizontally — set `x[0].bin`; better for many bins

options.name: BoxPlotV
options.when: Compare the spread, median and quartiles of several groups, vertically

options.name: BoxPlotH
options.when: Same as BoxPlotV with long group labels

options.name: ScatterPlot
options.when: Two-dimensional density — set `x.bin` or `y.bin` for a binned heatmap

decisionTree.question: What is the interval, or the movement between two states?

options.name: RangePlot
options.when: A static min–max interval per category, drawn as a dumbbell

options.name: CometPlot
options.when: Movement from one value to another per category, with direction shown by a tapered tail

options.name: BoxPlotH
options.when: The interval is a statistical summary (quartiles and median), not a plain min–max

decisionTree.question: How does a single value stand against its target?

options.name: BulletChart
options.when: One metric against base, target, threshold and max — the most information-dense option

options.name: LinearGauge
options.when: One value on a plain linear scale, optionally with an error value; compact enough for a table cell

options.name: RingGauge
options.when: Several metrics each against their own target, as concentric rings

options.name: SpeedometerChart
options.when: One value where a dial metaphor and coloured regions aid reading

options.name: PizzaChart
options.when: Several metrics of one entity against a shared max, as radial slices

decisionTree.question: How do entities compare across many metrics at once?

options.name: RadarChart
options.when: Five or more metrics on a shared scale, comparing a few entities by shape

options.name: PizzaChart
options.when: A single entity profiled across metrics, no entity-to-entity comparison

options.name: RingGauge
options.when: Metrics have individual targets rather than one shared scale

options.name: LineChart
options.when: Rank over time as a bump chart — convert values with `utils.convertToRanks` and use `curve: "bumpX"`

options.name: BarChart
options.when: A single ranked snapshot, sorted by value

decisionTree.question: When did events happen, and for how long?

options.name: TimeLineChart
options.when: Events or durations per row on a shared time axis, e.g. call logs or Gantt-style spans

options.name: Network
options.when: Nodes and edges, force-directed by default and optionally pinned to x/y scales

charts.name: AreaChart
charts.summary: Plots series as filled bands over a shared axis, showing a trend and the composition of a total at the same time.

encodings.description: Single key for the shared axis, typically time or period.
Array of series configs, one per band, drawn bottom-up in the order given.

useWhen: Both the overall trend and each series’ share of it need to be visible at once
Series are stacked parts of a meaningful total, e.g. revenue by product line
Relative share matters more than absolute values — set `stacking.type: "100%"`
A single series should read as volume or magnitude rather than a bare line
avoidWhen: Series need to be compared precisely against each other — stacked bands make all but the bottom one hard to read; use LineChart
Series can be negative and would overlap confusingly — use LineChart, or `stacking.type: "diverging"`
The x axis is categorical rather than continuous — use ColumnChartStacked
There is a single series and no notion of a total — use LineChart

alternatives.name: LineChart
alternatives.when: series must be compared precisely, or there is no meaningful total

alternatives.name: ColumnChartStacked
alternatives.when: the x axis is categorical rather than continuous

alternatives.name: PieChart
alternatives.when: showing composition at one point in time only

charts.example:
<AreaChart
  id="revenue-by-product"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'text-purple-900' },
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'text-purple-700' },
    { key: 'ipad', className: 'text-purple-500' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Streamgraph
variants.summary: A stacked area chart with a centred, flowing baseline instead of a flat one, emphasising the shape of each band over its exact value.
variants.how: Set `stacking={{ type: "streamgraph" }}`. Bands are ordered inside-out and offset by wiggle.
useWhen: Many series need showing over a long span and the rise and fall of each is the story
Relative movement matters more than reading any single value
The total is large and volatile, so a flat baseline would waste vertical space
avoidWhen: Any value must be read off the chart — no band sits on a fixed baseline; use a plain stacked AreaChart
There are only two or three series — the organic shape adds nothing over a normal stack
The audience needs the total, which a wiggle baseline obscures
variants.example:
<AreaChart
  id="genre-streamgraph"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'text-purple-900' },
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'text-purple-700' },
    { key: 'ipad', className: 'text-purple-500' },
  ]}
  stacking={{ type: 'streamgraph' }}
/>

variants.name: 100% stacked area chart
variants.summary: A stacked area chart normalised so every period fills the full height, showing share rather than absolute value.
variants.how: Set `stacking={{ type: "100%" }}`. The y axis becomes 0–100% of the period total.
useWhen: The mix matters and the absolute total does not
Totals differ so much between periods that a plain stack would hide the smaller ones
Showing how composition shifted over time, e.g. market share
avoidWhen: The total is part of the story — normalising deletes it; use a plain stacked AreaChart
A shrinking absolute value could be mistaken for a growing one because its share rose
variants.example:
<AreaChart
  id="market-share"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'text-purple-900' },
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'text-purple-700' },
  ]}
  stacking={{ type: '100%' }}
/>

variants.name: Diverging area chart
variants.summary: A stacked area chart that splits around a zero baseline, stacking positive series upward and negative ones downward.
variants.how: Set `stacking={{ type: "diverging" }}`. Series order is reversed so positive and negative stacks mirror each other.
useWhen: Series contain both gains and losses that should stack away from zero
Net position against zero is the message, e.g. inflows against outflows
avoidWhen: All values share a sign — the diverging offset then behaves as a plain stack with confusing ordering
variants.example:
<AreaChart
  id="flows"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'inflow', className: 'text-green-700' },
    { key: 'outflow', className: 'text-red-700' },
  ]}
  stacking={{ type: 'diverging' }}
/>

variants.name: Time-scaled area chart
variants.summary: An area chart whose x axis parses real dates rather than treating the key as a plain number.
variants.how: Set `x.scalingFunction: "time"` with `x.time.format`, or `x.time.isISO` for ISO strings.
useWhen: The x values are dates and the spacing between them is uneven
Axis ticks should fall on real date boundaries
variants.example:
<AreaChart
  id="daily-volume"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'date', scalingFunction: 'time', time: { isISO: true } }}
  y={[{ key: 'volume', className: 'text-blue-500' }]}
/>

charts.name: BarChart
charts.summary: Horizontal bars comparing one or more measures across categories, with room for long category labels.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row; becomes the vertical axis.
Array of numeric keys; one bar per key per category. Each entry also takes `rx` for rounded ends.

rowCount.note: Past ~40 rows the chart needs scrolling — bin the values instead.

useWhen: Category labels are long enough that vertical bars would truncate or rotate them
There are more categories than vertical bars can hold (roughly 12 or more)
Presenting a ranked list, sorted by value
Showing a histogram horizontally — set `bin` on the first `x` entry and bar lengths become counts
Bars should grow leftward from the right edge — set `direction: "left"`
avoidWhen: The x axis is time — a horizontal bar per period breaks the reading order; use LineChart or ColumnChart
Measures are parts of a whole — use BarChartStacked so the total is readable
Labels are short and there are few categories — ColumnChart is the more conventional read
Two measures should read outward from a shared centre — use SpineChart

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: few categories with short labels

alternatives.name: BarChartStacked
alternatives.when: measures are parts of a whole

alternatives.name: LollipopHChart
alternatives.when: bars look heavy and the value point is the focus

alternatives.name: SpineChart
alternatives.when: two opposing measures per category

charts.example:
<BarChart
  id="sales-by-region"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'region' }}
  x={[{ key: 'revenue', className: 'fill-blue-500' }]}
/>

variants.name: Horizontal histogram
variants.summary: Bins raw continuous values and draws the count per bin as horizontal bars, with bin ranges as labels down the y axis.
variants.how: Set `bin` on the first `x` entry: `x={[{ key: "score", bin: { count: 8 } }]}`. Bin labels move to the y axis automatically.
useWhen: A distribution has many bins, which fit better stacked vertically than squeezed across
Bin range labels are long, e.g. "10,000–20,000"
avoidWhen: The conventional histogram orientation is expected — use ColumnChart with `x.bin`
The x values are already categorical rather than continuous
variants.example:
<BarChart
  id="score-histogram"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={rawRows}
  x={[{ key: 'score', bin: { count: 8 }, className: 'fill-blue-500' }]}
  y={{ key: 'count' }}
/>

variants.name: Diverging bar chart
variants.summary: Bars growing left and right of a zero baseline, with negative values styled separately to show direction of change.
variants.how: Supply negative values in the data, set `start`/`end` on the series to pin a symmetric axis, and style with `className` plus `classNameNegative`.
useWhen: Values are changes against a baseline and the sign is the message, e.g. year-on-year delta
Gains and losses should be distinguishable at a glance by colour and direction
avoidWhen: All values share a sign — nothing diverges, so use a plain BarChart
The two directions are separate measures rather than one signed measure — use SpineChart
variants.example:
<BarChart
  id="yoy-change"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={[{
    key: 'delta',
    className: 'text-green-500',
    classNameNegative: 'text-red-500',
    start: -10,
    end: 10,
    axis: { location: 'top' },
  }]}
  y={{ key: 'year', padding: 10 }}
/>

variants.name: Data labels
variants.how: Pass `dataLabel={{ className: "fill-white text-xs" }}` to print values on the bars.

variants.name: Right-to-left
variants.how: Set `direction="left"` to anchor bars at the right edge.

charts.name: BarChartStacked
charts.summary: Horizontal bars where measures stack end to end, showing the total per category and its breakdown.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row.
Array of numeric keys, stacked left to right in the order given.

useWhen: Composition needs comparing across categories whose labels are long
Both the total and the proportions within each bar matter
Showing a waterfall of running gains and losses — set `waterfall`
avoidWhen: Segments need precise comparison across categories — only the first segment shares a baseline; use BarChart grouped
Labels are short and few — ColumnChartStacked reads more conventionally
There is one category only — use PieChart

alternatives.name: BarChart
alternatives.when: segments must be compared precisely rather than summed

alternatives.name: ColumnChartStacked
alternatives.when: short labels and few categories

alternatives.name: PieChart
alternatives.when: a single whole at one point in time

charts.example:
<BarChartStacked
  id="revenue-by-region"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'year' }}
  x={[
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'fill-purple-800' },
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'fill-purple-600' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Horizontal waterfall chart
variants.summary: Floating horizontal bars where each segment continues from the previous total, showing how a figure is built up step by step.
variants.how: Set `waterfall` on a BarChartStacked. Each `x` series becomes a step rather than a segment stacked from the baseline.
useWhen: Explaining a running total through successive gains and losses, where step labels are long
The sequence reads better vertically down the page than across it
avoidWhen: The series are independent categories with no running total — use a plain BarChart
Labels are short, in which case ColumnChartStacked in waterfall mode is the conventional read
variants.example:
<BarChartStacked
  id="profit-walk"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  waterfall
  y={{ key: 'year' }}
  x={[
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'fill-green-600' },
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'fill-red-500' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Reference lines
variants.how: Pass `referenceLines` to mark targets across the value axis.

variants.name: Data labels
variants.how: Pass `dataLabel` to print segment values inside the bars.

charts.name: ColumnChart
charts.summary: Vertical bars comparing one or more measures across categories; grouped side by side when several measures are passed.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row.
Array of numeric keys; one bar per key per category, drawn as a group.

seriesCount.note: Groups wider than ~4 bars get hard to scan.

rowCount.note: Past ~20 categories the labels collide — switch to BarChart.

useWhen: Comparing a numeric measure across a modest number of categories with short labels
Several measures need comparing within each category, side by side
The categories are periods (years, quarters) and individual values matter more than the trend line
Showing a histogram of raw continuous values — set `x.bin` and pass `y={[{ key: "count" }]}`
avoidWhen: Category labels are long or there are more than ~20 categories — use BarChart, where horizontal bars give labels room
The measures are parts of one whole — use ColumnChartStacked so the total is readable
The x axis is continuous time with many points — use LineChart
The bars would be nearly equal in height, making differences invisible — use LollipopVChart or a dot-based chart

alternatives.name: BarChart
alternatives.when: long labels or many categories

alternatives.name: ColumnChartStacked
alternatives.when: measures are parts of a whole

alternatives.name: LollipopVChart
alternatives.when: bars look heavy and values are the focus

alternatives.name: LineChart
alternatives.when: the axis is continuous time with many points

charts.example:
<ColumnChart
  id="sales-by-year"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'fill-purple-800' },
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'fill-purple-600' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Histogram
variants.summary: Bins raw continuous values into ranges and plots how many records fall into each, showing the shape of a distribution.
variants.how: Set `x={{ key: "score", bin: { count: 8 } }}` and `y={[{ key: "count" }]}`. Pass the raw rows as `data` — binning and counting happen internally. Use `bin.thresholds` for explicit edges.
useWhen: The data is raw measurements and the question is how they are spread, not what each one is
Skew, spread, gaps or multiple peaks need to be visible
Bin width should be tuned to reveal structure — adjust `bin.count`
avoidWhen: The x values are already categories — a histogram bins continuous data; use a plain ColumnChart
Groups need comparing by their summary statistics rather than their full shape — use BoxPlotV
There are too few records for bin heights to mean anything
variants.example:
<ColumnChart
  id="score-histogram"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={rawRows}
  x={{ key: 'score', bin: { count: 8 }, axis: { label: 'Score' } }}
  y={[{ key: 'count', className: 'text-blue-500' }]}
/>

variants.name: Reference lines
variants.how: Pass `referenceLines={[{ y: 50, className: "stroke-red-500" }]}`.

variants.name: Whole numbers
variants.how: Set `wholeNumbers` to force integer ticks on the value axis.

charts.name: ColumnChartStacked
charts.summary: Vertical bars where each measure stacks on the previous one, showing both the total per category and its composition.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row.
Array of numeric keys, stacked bottom-up in the order given.

useWhen: The total per category matters as much as its breakdown
Segments are genuinely parts of one whole, not independent measures
Showing a waterfall of running gains and losses — set `waterfall`
avoidWhen: Individual segments need precise comparison across categories — only the bottom segment shares a baseline; use ColumnChart grouped
Category labels are long or numerous — use BarChartStacked
There is one category only — use PieChart
The axis is continuous time — use AreaChart, which reads as a flow rather than discrete totals

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: segments must be compared precisely across categories

alternatives.name: BarChartStacked
alternatives.when: long category labels

alternatives.name: AreaChart
alternatives.when: the axis is continuous time

alternatives.name: PieChart
alternatives.when: a single whole at one point in time

charts.example:
<ColumnChartStacked
  id="revenue-split"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'fill-purple-800' },
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'fill-purple-600' },
    { key: 'ipad', className: 'fill-purple-400' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Waterfall chart
variants.summary: Floating columns where each segment starts where the previous one ended, showing how a running total is built up from successive gains and losses.
variants.how: Set `waterfall` on a ColumnChartStacked. Each `y` series becomes a step in the sequence rather than a segment stacked from the baseline.
useWhen: Explaining how a starting figure becomes an ending figure through a sequence of contributions
Each step is a gain or a loss against a running total, e.g. revenue bridge or profit walk
The order of the steps carries meaning and should be read left to right
avoidWhen: The series are independent categories with no running total — use a plain grouped ColumnChart
The order of steps is arbitrary, which makes the bridge metaphor meaningless
Category labels are long — use BarChartStacked in waterfall mode instead
variants.example:
<ColumnChartStacked
  id="revenue-bridge"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  waterfall
  x={{ key: 'year' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'macbook', className: 'fill-green-600' },
    { key: 'iphone', className: 'fill-green-500' },
    { key: 'ipad', className: 'fill-red-500' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Reference lines
variants.how: Pass `referenceLines={[{ y: 100, className: "stroke-red-500" }]}`.

charts.name: LineChart
charts.summary: Plots one or more numeric series against a shared ordered or time axis to show how values move.

encodings.description: Single key for the shared axis. Set `scalingFunction: "time"` with `time.format` for dates; otherwise treated as linear.
Array of series configs, one per line. Each takes `className`, `curve`, `symbol` and an optional `axis.location: "right"` for a second scale.

seriesCount.note: Beyond ~8 lines the chart becomes a hairball; facet instead.

useWhen: The x axis is time or another continuous ordered dimension and the shape of the movement is the point
Several series must be compared against each other over the same axis
Two measures on different scales need separate left and right axes (set `axis.location: "right"` on the second series)
Gaps in the data should break the line — missing keys are skipped rather than zeroed
avoidWhen: The x axis is categorical with no inherent order — use ColumnChart or BarChart, since a line implies continuity that is not there
The split of a total matters as much as the trend — use AreaChart
There are only two or three points per series — use ColumnChart, where individual values are easier to read
The data is discrete events or durations rather than a measured value — use TimeLineChart

alternatives.name: AreaChart
alternatives.when: volume under the curve or composition of a total matters

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: few discrete periods, individual values matter more than the trend

alternatives.name: TimeLineChart
alternatives.when: plotting events and durations rather than a continuous measure

alternatives.name: ScatterPlot
alternatives.when: the x axis is a measure rather than time, and points should not be joined

charts.example:
<LineChart
  id="revenue-trend"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'month' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'revenue', className: 'text-blue-500' },
    { key: 'forecast', className: 'text-gray-400', curve: 'step' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Bump chart
variants.summary: Plots rank rather than value over time, so lines cross when entities overtake one another.
variants.how: Convert values to ranks with `utils.convertToRanks(data, y, x)` — it takes the same `y` array and `x` object you pass to the chart — then set `curve: "bumpX"` and `label: { show: true }` on each series, and `reverse` so rank 1 sits at the top.
useWhen: Changes in ordering are the story, not the size of the underlying values
Entities are closely bunched, so a value chart would be an unreadable tangle
Overtaking events should be visible as line crossings
avoidWhen: The size of the gap between entities matters — ranking discards magnitude entirely; use a plain LineChart
There are too many entities for the crossings to be followable

variants.name: Step chart
variants.summary: Joins points with horizontal and vertical segments rather than diagonals, showing a value that holds constant then jumps.
variants.how: Set `curve: "step"` on each series.
useWhen: The value genuinely holds constant between readings, e.g. a price or a rate that changes at discrete moments
Interpolating between points would imply change that did not happen
avoidWhen: The underlying quantity varies continuously — a step then misrepresents it; use the default line
variants.example:
<LineChart
  id="rate-changes"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'date' }}
  y={[{ key: 'rate', curve: 'step', className: 'text-blue-500' }]}
/>

variants.name: Dual-axis line chart
variants.summary: Plots two series against independent left and right scales so measures in different units can share one plot.
variants.how: Give the second series `axis: { location: "right" }` and widen `margin.right`. Label the scales with `yLeftLabel` and `yRightLabel`.
useWhen: Two related measures use different units or magnitudes, e.g. revenue and conversion rate
The correlation in shape between the two is the point
avoidWhen: The two scales could be made comparable — independent axes let any two series be made to look correlated by choosing scales
More than two measures are involved; a third scale is unreadable
variants.example:
<LineChart
  id="revenue-vs-rate"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  margin={{ right: 40 }}
  yLeftLabel="Revenue"
  yRightLabel="Conversion"
  x={{ key: 'month' }}
  y={[
    { key: 'revenue', className: 'text-green-500' },
    { key: 'conversion', className: 'text-blue-500', axis: { location: 'right' } },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Time-scaled line chart
variants.summary: A line chart whose x axis parses real dates rather than treating the key as a plain number.
variants.how: Set `x.scalingFunction: "time"` and `x.time.format` (or `x.time.isISO`) to parse date strings.
useWhen: The x values are dates and the gaps between them are uneven
Ticks should land on real date boundaries rather than arbitrary numbers
variants.example:
<LineChart
  id="daily-signups"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'date', scalingFunction: 'time', time: { isISO: true } }}
  y={[{ key: 'signups', className: 'text-blue-500' }]}
/>

variants.name: Curved lines
variants.how: Set `curve: "rounded"` for Catmull-Rom smoothing, or `"line"` for plain straight segments.

variants.name: Reference lines
variants.how: Pass `referenceLines={[{ yLeft: 100, className: "stroke-red-500" }]}`.

charts.name: LollipopHChart
charts.summary: Horizontal stems ending in a symbol, marking one value per category with far less ink than a bar.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row.
Single numeric key. Set `start: 0` to anchor stems at zero.
Symbol at the end of each stem: circle (default), diamond, triangle, square, cross, star or wye.

seriesCount.note: One value per category; use BarChart for multiple measures.

rowCount.note: Lollipops stay legible where bars would look like a solid block.

useWhen: There are many categories and a wall of bars would look heavy
The exact value point matters more than the magnitude-as-area a bar implies
Category labels are long enough to need horizontal orientation
Values are clustered in a narrow band where bar lengths would look nearly identical
avoidWhen: Several measures need comparing per category — a lollipop carries one value; use BarChart
The magnitude should read as accumulated quantity — bars encode that better
The axis is time — use LineChart
A vertical layout is wanted — use LollipopVChart

alternatives.name: BarChart
alternatives.when: multiple measures per category, or magnitude should read as area

alternatives.name: LollipopVChart
alternatives.when: a vertical layout fits the space better

alternatives.name: RangePlot
alternatives.when: each category has an interval rather than a single value

charts.example:
<LollipopHChart
  id="scores-by-team"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'name' }}
  x={{ key: 'value', start: 0 }}
/>

variants.name: Custom symbol
variants.how: Pass `shape="diamond"` (or star, triangle, square, cross, wye).

variants.name: Axis labels
variants.how: Set `x.axis.label` and `y.axis.label` to title each axis.

variants.name: Styling
variants.how: Use `classNames.classNameLines` and `classNames.classNameSymbols` to style stems and heads separately.

charts.name: LollipopVChart
charts.summary: Vertical stems ending in a symbol, marking one value per category with far less ink than a column.

encodings.description: Single key holding the category label for each row.
Single numeric key. Set `start: 0` to anchor stems at zero.
Symbol at the end of each stem: circle, diamond, triangle, square, cross, star or wye. Unlike LollipopHChart this prop has no default.

useWhen: A column chart would look heavy but the vertical orientation should be kept
The value point matters more than magnitude-as-area
Category labels are short enough to sit under vertical stems
avoidWhen: Several measures need comparing per category — use ColumnChart
Category labels are long — use LollipopHChart
The axis is continuous time — use LineChart

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: multiple measures per category, or magnitude should read as area

alternatives.name: LollipopHChart
alternatives.when: category labels are long

alternatives.name: ScatterPlot
alternatives.when: both axes are numeric rather than one being categorical

charts.example:
<LollipopVChart
  id="readings-by-name"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  shape="circle"
  x={{ key: 'name', axis: { location: 'bottom' } }}
  y={{ key: 'reading', start: 0, axis: { location: 'left' } }}
/>

variants.name: Custom symbol
variants.how: Pass `shape="star"` (or diamond, triangle, square, cross, wye).

variants.name: Styling
variants.how: Use `classNames.classNameLines` and `classNames.classNameSymbols` to style stems and heads separately.

variants.name: Fixed value range
variants.how: Pass `valueMin` and `valueMax` to pin the value axis.

charts.name: SpineChart
charts.summary: Bars growing outward in both directions from a shared centre axis, comparing opposing measures per category.

encodings.description: Single key for the category label. Set `axis.location: "middle"` to put labels on the spine itself, or "left"/"right" to move them aside.
Array of numeric keys, each with `direction: "left" | "right"` deciding which side of the spine it grows toward.

useWhen: Two groups are being contrasted on the same measure, e.g. a population pyramid by sex or this year against last
The symmetry of the split is itself the message
Categories share a scale and both sides should be read against the same axis
avoidWhen: There is no natural opposition between the measures — the mirrored layout implies one; use BarChart
More than a few measures per side are needed — the spine gets crowded; use BarChart grouped
The measures are parts of one whole rather than two sides — use BarChartStacked

alternatives.name: BarChart
alternatives.when: the measures are not naturally opposed

alternatives.name: BarChartStacked
alternatives.when: the measures are parts of one whole

alternatives.name: CometPlot
alternatives.when: showing movement between two states rather than two independent measures

charts.example:
<SpineChart
  id="population-pyramid"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'ageGroup', axis: { location: 'middle' } }}
  x={[
    { key: 'male', direction: 'left', className: 'fill-blue-700' },
    { key: 'female', direction: 'right', className: 'fill-pink-500' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Labels aside
variants.how: Set `y.axis.location` to "left" or "right" to move category labels off the spine.

variants.name: Centre gap
variants.how: Use `margin.middle` to widen the gap between the two sides.

variants.name: Axis on top
variants.how: Set `xAxis="top"` to move the value axis above the plot.

charts.name: TimeLineChart
charts.summary: Places discrete events and durations on a shared time axis, one lane per category.

encodings.description: Key whose values become the lanes (rows) of the timeline.
Key holding the event start. Set `events.isTime` when the values are dates.
Key holding the event end. Omit for point events rather than spans.
Key selecting the mark per event via `shapeMapping` — circle, rect or line.

rowCount.note: One lane per distinct y value.

useWhen: The data is events with timestamps rather than a measured value sampled over time
Durations need to be visible as spans — pass both `startKey` and `endKey`
Activity should be compared across lanes, e.g. calls per line, jobs per worker
Building a Gantt-style view of overlapping work
avoidWhen: A continuous quantity is being tracked over time — use LineChart or AreaChart
Only counts per period matter, not individual events — aggregate and use ColumnChart
There is no time dimension at all — this chart has no meaning without one

alternatives.name: LineChart
alternatives.when: tracking a measured value over time rather than discrete events

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: event counts per period are enough

alternatives.name: RangePlot
alternatives.when: intervals are numeric ranges rather than moments in time

charts.example:
<TimeLineChart
  id="call-timeline"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'agent' }}
  events={{
    startKey: 'callStartTime',
    endKey: 'callEndTime',
    isTime: true,
  }}
/>

variants.name: Gantt chart
variants.summary: Draws each row’s work as a horizontal bar spanning its start and end dates, one lane per resource or task.
variants.how: Pass both `events.startKey` and `events.endKey` with `events.isTime: true`, and set `y` to the lane key. Spans render as rects; overlapping work in a lane is visible as stacked bars.
useWhen: Work has a start and an end and the overlap between items is the question
Scheduling, capacity or utilisation needs to be read per lane
Durations differ enough that their relative length carries meaning
avoidWhen: Items are instants rather than spans — omit `endKey` for a point-event timeline instead
Dependencies between tasks are the real subject; this chart draws no links between bars
variants.example:
<TimeLineChart
  id="project-gantt"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={tasks}
  y={{ key: 'owner' }}
  events={{
    startKey: 'start',
    endKey: 'end',
    isTime: true,
    classNameKey: 'status',
    classNameMapping: { done: 'fill-green-500', active: 'fill-blue-500' },
  }}
/>

variants.name: Point events
variants.how: Omit `events.endKey` and set `events.sizeKey` to size circular markers.

variants.name: Mixed marks
variants.how: Set `events.shapeKey` with `events.shapeMapping` to draw circle, rect or line per event type.

variants.name: Colour by type
variants.how: Set `events.classNameKey` with `events.classNameMapping`.

charts.name: PieChart
charts.summary: Divides a circle into slices sized by value, showing how much each category contributes to one whole.

encodings.description: Key holding the slice label.
Key holding the slice size. Values are summed to form the whole.
Maps each name value to a fill class; nothing is coloured by default.

rowCount.note: Beyond ~8 slices, angles stop being distinguishable.

useWhen: The values are parts of a single whole and sum to something meaningful
There are roughly six or fewer categories
The rough share of one or two dominant slices is the message, not precise comparison
A seating or parliament metaphor fits — set `startAngle`/`endAngle` for a semicircle
avoidWhen: Slices need precise comparison — angles are read far less accurately than lengths; use BarChart or ColumnChart
The values do not sum to a meaningful whole, e.g. independent metrics or averages
Composition must be compared across categories or over time — use ColumnChartStacked or AreaChart
Any value is negative — a slice cannot represent it

alternatives.name: ColumnChartStacked
alternatives.when: composition compared across several categories or periods

alternatives.name: BarChart
alternatives.when: slices need precise comparison

alternatives.name: WaffleChart
alternatives.when: part-to-whole shown as countable cells rather than angles

charts.example:
<PieChart
  id="revenue-share"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  nameKey="product"
  valueKey="revenue"
  classNameMap={{ macbook: 'fill-purple-300', iphone: 'fill-purple-800' }}
/>

variants.name: Donut chart
variants.summary: A pie chart with a hollow centre, which reads share by arc length rather than by wedge area and frees the middle for a total.
variants.how: Set `innerRadius` above 0. Values are a fraction of `outerRadius`, so `innerRadius={0.5}` hollows half the radius.
useWhen: The same part-to-whole story as a pie, but the centre should carry a headline figure or label
Slices are thin and the reduced centre clutter helps
avoidWhen: Precise comparison is needed — a donut is no more accurate than a pie; use BarChart
There are many slices, which a donut makes harder to read rather than easier
variants.example:
<PieChart
  id="revenue-donut"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  nameKey="product"
  valueKey="revenue"
  innerRadius={0.5}
  cornerRadius={4}
  paddingAngle={2}
/>

variants.name: Semicircle chart
variants.summary: A pie swept through 180° rather than 360°, echoing a parliamentary seating plan.
variants.how: Set `startAngle={-90}` and `endAngle={90}`. Combine with `innerRadius` for a half donut.
useWhen: Showing seat shares, poll results or any split with a parliamentary metaphor
The chart must sit in a wide, short space where a full circle would not fit
avoidWhen: There is no seating or directional metaphor — the half circle then just halves the resolution for no reason
variants.example:
<PieChart
  id="seat-share"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  nameKey="party"
  valueKey="seats"
  startAngle={-90}
  endAngle={90}
/>

variants.name: Rounded slices
variants.how: Set `cornerRadius` and `paddingAngle` to separate and round the slices.

variants.name: Unsorted
variants.how: Set `sort={false}` to keep data order instead of sorting by value descending.

charts.name: ScatterPlot
charts.summary: One point per record positioned by two measures, revealing correlation, clusters and outliers.

encodings.description: Numeric key for the horizontal position.
Numeric key for the vertical position.
Categorical key plus a `classNameMap` to colour points by group.
Numeric key plus `min`/`max` radius to encode a third measure as bubble size.
Second categorical key plus a `shapeMap`, useful for accessibility alongside colour.

rowCount.note: Past a few thousand points, bin into a heatmap.

useWhen: The question is whether and how two measures move together
Outliers or clusters need to be visible as individual records
Up to five dimensions must share one plot — x, y, size, colour and shape
Points should be joined in data order to show a path over time — set `connect.enabled`
Point density matters more than individual records — set `x.bin` or `y.bin` for a binned heatmap
avoidWhen: One axis is categorical rather than numeric — use ColumnChart or a lollipop chart
There are only a handful of records — a table or bar chart communicates more directly
Overplotting hides the pattern — switch to the binned heatmap mode or use WaffleChart
The x axis is time and the sequence is the point — use LineChart

alternatives.name: WaffleChart
alternatives.when: both axes are categorical or binned and density is the message

alternatives.name: LineChart
alternatives.when: x is time and the sequence matters

alternatives.name: BoxPlotV
alternatives.when: comparing the spread of a measure across groups rather than two measures

charts.example:
<ScatterPlot
  id="gdp-vs-power"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'gdp' }}
  y={{ key: 'purchasing_power' }}
  color={{ key: 'continent', classNameMap: { Asia: 'fill-red-600', Europe: 'fill-blue-600' } }}
/>

variants.name: Bubble chart
variants.summary: A scatter plot whose point radius encodes a third measure, showing three quantities at once.
variants.how: Add `size={{ key: "population", min: 2, max: 20 }}`. Radius is scaled between `min` and `max` pixels.
useWhen: A third numeric dimension matters — classically GDP against life expectancy sized by population
The relative weight of each point should temper how the x/y pattern is read
avoidWhen: The third measure needs reading precisely — area is judged poorly; use colour or a second chart
Points are dense enough that large bubbles would occlude each other
variants.example:
<ScatterPlot
  id="gdp-bubbles"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'gdp' }}
  y={{ key: 'life_expectancy' }}
  size={{ key: 'population', min: 3, max: 24 }}
  color={{ key: 'continent', classNameMap: { Asia: 'fill-red-600' } }}
/>

variants.name: Connected scatterplot
variants.summary: A scatter plot whose points are joined in data order, tracing the path two measures took together.
variants.how: Set `connect={{ enabled: true, className: "stroke-gray-400" }}`. Points join in the order the data is given, so sort it first.
useWhen: Two measures evolve together over time and the trajectory is the story
Loops or reversals in the relationship should be visible, which a plain scatter hides
avoidWhen: The data has no meaningful order — the connecting line invents a sequence that does not exist
Only one measure changes over time; use LineChart
variants.example:
<ScatterPlot
  id="phillips-curve"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={sortedByYear}
  x={{ key: 'unemployment' }}
  y={{ key: 'inflation' }}
  connect={{ enabled: true, className: 'stroke-gray-400' }}
/>

variants.name: Density heatmap
variants.summary: Bins points into a grid and colours each cell by how many fell into it, revealing density where individual points would overplot.
variants.how: Set `x.bin` and/or `y.bin`. Cells show counts, coloured via `binColor.scale` with an optional `binColor.domain`.
useWhen: There are too many points to plot individually without them merging into a solid mass
Where the data concentrates matters more than any individual record
avoidWhen: Outliers are the point — binning buries a single distant record in a pale cell; use a plain ScatterPlot
There are few enough points to show individually
variants.example:
<ScatterPlot
  id="density"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'gdp', bin: { count: 12 } }}
  y={{ key: 'purchasing_power', bin: { count: 12 } }}
  binColor={{ scale: interpolateBlues }}
/>

variants.name: Zooming
variants.how: Set `zooming={{ enabled: true, min: 1, max: 8 }}` for scroll-to-zoom.

variants.name: Click handling
variants.how: Pass `onClick={(event, d) => …}` to react to point selection.

charts.name: WaffleChart
charts.summary: A grid of cells indexed by two categorical axes, with a third value encoded as cell colour — a heatmap.

encodings.description: Key whose unique values become columns. Set `bin` to group a continuous field instead.
Key whose unique values become rows. Set `bin` to group a continuous field instead.
Key holding the cell value, plus a D3 sequential `scale` (e.g. `interpolateBlues`) or a `classNameMap` for discrete colours.

useWhen: Two categorical dimensions cross and a magnitude sits at each intersection, e.g. month by year
The pattern across the whole grid matters more than any single value
Cyclical structure should be visible, such as seasonality down rows and drift across columns
Raw continuous data needs binning on one or both axes — set `x.bin`/`y.bin` and cells show counts
avoidWhen: Precise values must be read off — colour is the least precise encoding; use a table or BarChart
One axis is continuous and unbinned — use ScatterPlot
There are only a few categories, where a grid is overkill — use ColumnChart
The grid would be mostly empty — sparse heatmaps read as noise

alternatives.name: ScatterPlot
alternatives.when: axes are continuous measures rather than categories

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: only one categorical dimension is involved

alternatives.name: PieChart
alternatives.when: showing part-to-whole for a single set of categories

charts.example:
<WaffleChart
  id="temps-by-month"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year', axis: { location: 'bottom', label: 'Year' } }}
  y={{ key: 'month', axis: { location: 'left', label: 'Month' } }}
  color={{ key: 'temperature', scale: interpolateRdYlGn }}
/>

variants.name: Calendar heatmap
variants.summary: A heatmap with time units on both axes — months down, years across — so seasonal cycles and long-run drift are visible at once.
variants.how: Map the finer time unit to `y` and the coarser to `x`, then colour by the measure. Use a diverging scale such as `interpolateRdYlGn` for values with a meaningful middle.
useWhen: The data is one value per period over several cycles, e.g. monthly temperature across years
Both the within-year pattern and the across-year trend need to be readable in one view
avoidWhen: Only the trend matters, with no cyclical structure — use LineChart
Periods are missing, which leaves holes that read as data rather than absence
variants.example:
<WaffleChart
  id="temps-calendar"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'year', axis: { location: 'bottom', label: 'Year' } }}
  y={{ key: 'month', axis: { location: 'left', label: 'Month' } }}
  color={{ key: 'temperature', scale: interpolateRdYlGn }}
/>

variants.name: Binned 2D histogram
variants.summary: Groups raw continuous values into ranges on both axes and colours each cell by how many records fall in it.
variants.how: Set `bin` on `x` and/or `y`; each cell then shows the count for that (xBin, yBin) pair rather than a value from the data.
useWhen: Both axes are continuous and the joint distribution is the question
Point-level detail is unnecessary or would overplot
avoidWhen: Individual records must stay identifiable — use ScatterPlot
One axis is already categorical, in which case bin only the other
variants.example:
<WaffleChart
  id="joint-distribution"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={rawRows}
  x={{ key: 'height', bin: { count: 8 } }}
  y={{ key: 'weight', bin: { count: 8 } }}
  color={{ key: 'count', scale: interpolateBlues }}
/>

variants.name: Discrete colours
variants.how: Use `color.classNameMap` instead of `color.scale` to map values to CSS classes.

variants.name: Rounded cells
variants.how: Set `rx` for rounded corners and `gap` for spacing between cells.

charts.name: BoxPlotH
charts.summary: Horizontal box-and-whisker marks summarising the spread of a measure per group: min, quartiles, median and max.

encodings.description: Key holding the group label; one box per group. Set `bin` here to group a continuous field into bands instead.
Config naming the statistic keys: `minKey`, `maxKey`, `midKey`, `boxStart` and `boxEnd`. When `y.bin` is set these are computed internally and can be omitted.
With `y.bin` set, names the raw continuous field the box statistics are computed from.

useWhen: The spread of a measure needs comparing across groups, not just its average
Median and quartiles matter — an average alone would hide skew
Group labels are long enough to need horizontal orientation
Statistics should be derived from raw rows — set `y.bin` with `valueKey` and they are computed automatically
avoidWhen: Every underlying point should be visible — use ScatterPlot
The interval is a plain min–max rather than a statistical summary — use RangePlot
The audience will not read quartiles; a histogram via ColumnChart with `x.bin` is more intuitive
A vertical layout fits better — use BoxPlotV

alternatives.name: BoxPlotV
alternatives.when: a vertical layout fits the space better

alternatives.name: RangePlot
alternatives.when: showing a plain min–max interval rather than quartiles

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: a histogram of one group is enough — set `x.bin`

charts.example:
<BoxPlotH
  id="scores-by-team"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'name' }}
  x={{
    minKey: 'min',
    maxKey: 'max',
    midKey: 'mid',
    boxStart: 'firstQuartile',
    boxEnd: 'lastQuartile',
    min: 0,
  }}
/>

variants.name: Binned box plot
variants.summary: Bins a continuous field into groups and computes each group’s min, quartiles and median from the raw rows, rather than taking pre-aggregated statistics.
variants.how: Set `bin` on the `y` (category) config and pass `valueKey` naming the field to summarise. The statistic keys on `x` are then computed internally and can be omitted.
useWhen: The data is raw observations and the statistics have not been computed upstream
The grouping field is continuous, e.g. distribution of salary by age band
Bin boundaries need tuning to see how the distribution shifts across groups
avoidWhen: Groups are already categorical — pass them directly with a plain `y` key instead of binning
The statistics are already computed, in which case name the keys directly
variants.example:
<BoxPlotH
  id="salary-by-age"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={rawRows}
  valueKey="salary"
  y={{ key: 'age', bin: { count: 5 } }}
  x={{ min: 0 }}
/>

variants.name: Per-row colours
variants.how: Put a `className` field on each row to colour boxes individually.

charts.name: BoxPlotV
charts.summary: Vertical box-and-whisker marks summarising the spread of a measure per group: min, quartiles, median and max.

encodings.description: Key holding the group label; one box per group. Set `bin` here to group a continuous field into bands instead.
Config naming the statistic keys: `minKey`, `maxKey`, `midKey`, `boxStart` and `boxEnd`. When `x.bin` is set these are computed internally and can be omitted.
With `x.bin` set, names the raw continuous field the box statistics are computed from.

useWhen: The spread of a measure needs comparing across a few groups with short labels
Skew and outliers matter, so a mean alone would mislead
Groups are ordered periods and the change in spread over them is the message
Statistics should be derived from raw rows — set `x.bin` with `valueKey`
avoidWhen: Every underlying point should be visible — use ScatterPlot
The interval is a plain min–max — use RangePlot
Group labels are long — use BoxPlotH
Only the central value matters — use ColumnChart

alternatives.name: BoxPlotH
alternatives.when: group labels are long

alternatives.name: RangePlot
alternatives.when: showing a plain min–max interval rather than quartiles

alternatives.name: ScatterPlot
alternatives.when: individual records should stay visible

charts.example:
<BoxPlotV
  id="salary-by-band"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  x={{ key: 'name' }}
  y={{
    minKey: 'min',
    maxKey: 'max',
    midKey: 'mid',
    boxStart: 'firstQuartile',
    boxEnd: 'lastQuartile',
    min: 0,
  }}
/>

variants.name: Binned box plot (vertical)
aliases: vertical box plot from raw data
variants.summary: Bins a continuous field into groups along the x axis and computes each group’s quartiles from the raw rows.
variants.how: Set `bin` on the `x` (category) config and pass `valueKey` naming the field to summarise. The statistic keys on `y` are then computed internally and can be omitted. Use `bin.thresholds` for explicit band edges.
useWhen: The data is raw observations and no statistics have been computed upstream
The grouping field is continuous, e.g. salary distribution by age band
avoidWhen: Groups are already categorical — pass them directly rather than binning
The statistics are already computed, in which case name the keys directly
variants.example:
<BoxPlotV
  id="salary-by-age"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={rawRows}
  valueKey="salary"
  x={{ key: 'age', bin: { count: 5 }, axis: { label: 'Age Group' } }}
  y={{ min: 0, axis: { label: 'Salary' } }}
/>

variants.name: Per-row colours
variants.how: Put a `className` field on each row to colour boxes individually.

charts.name: CometPlot
charts.summary: A tapered mark per category running from one value to another, where the widening head shows the direction of movement.

encodings.description: Key holding the category label; one comet per row.
Config naming the endpoints: `fromKey` (tail) and `toKey` (head). The taper runs from tail to head.

useWhen: A value moved between two states and the direction of that move matters
Comparing before-and-after across categories, e.g. score with and without a change
The magnitude of change should read at a glance from the shape rather than from a computed delta
avoidWhen: The two values are an unordered interval with no direction — use RangePlot
The interval is a quartile summary — use BoxPlotH
More than two states are involved — use LineChart with one line per category

alternatives.name: RangePlot
alternatives.when: the interval has no direction

alternatives.name: LineChart
alternatives.when: more than two points in the sequence

alternatives.name: SpineChart
alternatives.when: contrasting two independent measures rather than a movement

charts.example:
<CometPlot
  id="score-change"
  className="w-full h-56"
  data={data}
  y={{ key: 'name' }}
  x={{ fromKey: 'before', toKey: 'after', className: 'fill-green-800 stroke-green-800' }}
/>

variants.name: Custom head
variants.how: Set `shape` to diamond, triangle, square, cross, star or wye, and `size` to scale it.

variants.name: Tail styling
variants.how: Use `x.classNameTail` to style the tail separately from the head.

charts.name: RangePlot
charts.summary: A dumbbell per category: two endpoints joined by a bar, showing the interval between a low and a high value.

encodings.description: Key holding the category label; one range per row.
Config naming the interval endpoints: `minKey` and `maxKey`. Pin the axis with `start` and `end`.

useWhen: Each category has a low and a high value and the gap between them is the message
Comparing spans across categories, e.g. min and max temperature per city
Showing a before-and-after pair where direction does not need emphasis
A box plot would overstate the statistical rigour of the data
avoidWhen: Direction of movement matters — use CometPlot, whose tapered tail shows which way the value moved
The interval is a statistical summary with quartiles — use BoxPlotH
Only one value per category exists — use LollipopHChart
The endpoints are times rather than numbers — use TimeLineChart

alternatives.name: CometPlot
alternatives.when: the direction of movement between the two values matters

alternatives.name: BoxPlotH
alternatives.when: the interval is a quartile summary

alternatives.name: LollipopHChart
alternatives.when: there is a single value per category

charts.example:
<RangePlot
  id="temp-range"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  shape="circle"
  y={{ key: 'label', axis: { location: 'left' } }}
  x={{ minKey: 'minTemp', maxKey: 'maxTemp', start: 0, end: 100 }}
/>

variants.name: Styling
variants.how: Use `classNameData` to style the connecting bar and endpoints.

variants.name: Fixed axis
variants.how: Set `x.start` and `x.end` to keep the scale stable across renders.

charts.name: BulletChart
charts.summary: A compact linear gauge showing one measure against a base, a target, a threshold and a maximum.

encodings.description: The single measured value.
Lower qualitative band, e.g. last period’s result.
The goal, drawn as a marker.
The point past which performance counts as good.
Top of the scale.
Text naming the metric.

useWhen: One KPI needs showing against a goal plus qualitative bands, in little vertical space
Several KPIs will be stacked in a dashboard column and must align on a common layout
A speedometer would waste space for the same information
avoidWhen: There is no target or threshold to compare against — use LinearGauge
Several metrics each have their own target and should read as one unit — use RingGauge
The value changes over time and the history matters — use LineChart
The data is an array of records rather than a single number — gauges take one value

alternatives.name: LinearGauge
alternatives.when: there is no target or threshold, just a value on a scale

alternatives.name: RingGauge
alternatives.when: several metrics each against their own target

alternatives.name: SpeedometerChart
alternatives.when: a dial metaphor suits the audience better

charts.example:
<BulletChart
  id="sales-vs-target"
  className="w-full h-24"
  data={85}
  label="Sales"
  min={0}
  base={50}
  target={80}
  threshold={90}
  max={100}
/>

variants.name: Styled bands
variants.how: Style each element with `classNameData`, `classNameTarget`, `classNameThreshold`, `classNameBase` and `classNameMax`.

variants.name: Live updates
variants.how: Change `data` on an interval; the bar animates when `drawing.duration` is set.

charts.name: LinearGauge
charts.summary: A single value drawn as a filled bar on a linear scale, with an optional error band.

encodings.description: The value to display. The scale runs 0 to `max`, which defaults to 1 — so pass a fraction unless `max` is set.
Text naming the metric; also accepts a D3 value function.
Top of the scale. Defaults to 1.
`{ data, className }` drawing an error or shortfall band at the top of the scale.

useWhen: A single value needs showing as a share of a total, with no target to compare against
The gauge must fit in a table cell, list row or card — it is the most compact chart here
An error or shortfall portion should be visible alongside the value
avoidWhen: There is a target, threshold or qualitative band to compare against — use BulletChart, which encodes all of them
Several related metrics should read as one unit — use RingGauge
History or trend matters — use LineChart

alternatives.name: BulletChart
alternatives.when: there is a target and threshold to show

alternatives.name: RingGauge
alternatives.when: several metrics each with their own target

alternatives.name: SpeedometerChart
alternatives.when: a dial metaphor with coloured regions suits better

charts.example:
<LinearGauge
  id="disk-usage"
  className="h-12"
  label="Disk usage"
  data={0.47}
/>

variants.name: Absolute scale
variants.how: Set `max={100}` and pass the raw value instead of a fraction.

variants.name: Error band
variants.how: Pass `error={{ data: 0.1, className: "fill-red-500" }}`.

variants.name: Styling
variants.how: Use `classNameGauge` for the fill and `classNameGaugeBg` for the track.

charts.name: PizzaChart
charts.summary: Equal-angle radial slices, one per metric, each extending from the centre in proportion to its value.

encodings.description: A single record — one object, not an array — holding every metric as a field.
Array of `{ key, className, classNameBackground }`, one slice per entry, in the order given.

useWhen: One entity is being profiled across several metrics that share a scale
The overall silhouette matters more than reading individual values
Slices have a natural order, so the shape is comparable between renders
avoidWhen: Several entities need comparing — a pizza shows one; use RadarChart, which overlays many
The metrics are parts of one whole — use PieChart, where angle encodes share
Precise values matter — radius is read poorly; use ColumnChart
Each metric has its own target rather than a shared max — use RingGauge

alternatives.name: RadarChart
alternatives.when: several entities must be compared across the same metrics

alternatives.name: RingGauge
alternatives.when: each metric has its own target

alternatives.name: PieChart
alternatives.when: the values are parts of one whole

charts.example:
<PizzaChart
  id="quality-profile"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={record}
  max={100}
  metrics={[
    { key: 'metric1', className: 'fill-purple-900' },
    { key: 'metric2', className: 'fill-purple-700' },
    { key: 'metric3', className: 'fill-purple-500' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Scale bounds
variants.how: Set `min` and `max` so slice radius is comparable across renders.

variants.name: Slice shaping
variants.how: Set `paddingAngle` and `cornerRadius` to separate and round slices.

variants.name: Backdrop
variants.how: Use `classNameBackground` per metric to show the unfilled remainder.

charts.name: RadarChart
charts.summary: Plots several metrics on spokes radiating from a centre and joins them into a polygon per entity, comparing profiles by shape.

encodings.description: `{ key }` naming the entity each polygon represents.
Array of `{ key }`, one spoke per entry. All metrics must share the `min`–`max` scale.
Maps each entity label to stroke and fill classes.

seriesCount.note: Spokes; fewer than 5 makes a shape too crude to compare.

rowCount.note: Overlapping polygons; past ~5 entities they obscure each other.

useWhen: Five or more metrics are compared across a few entities on one shared scale, such as 0–100
The profile shape is the message — which entity is strong or weak where
Metrics have a natural cyclical or grouped order that makes the shape meaningful
avoidWhen: Metrics use different units or ranges — one shared radial scale would misrepresent them; use ColumnChart grouped
More than about five entities need overlaying — the polygons become unreadable
Precise values must be compared — radial position is read poorly; use BarChart
Only one entity is being shown — use PizzaChart

alternatives.name: PizzaChart
alternatives.when: profiling a single entity

alternatives.name: ColumnChart
alternatives.when: metrics have different units, or values must be read precisely

alternatives.name: RingGauge
alternatives.when: each metric has its own target rather than a shared scale

charts.example:
<RadarChart
  id="team-profile"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={data}
  label={{ key: 'name' }}
  min={0}
  max={100}
  metrics={[
    { key: 'attack' },
    { key: 'defense' },
    { key: 'midfield' },
    { key: 'goalkeeper' },
    { key: 'overall' },
  ]}
/>

variants.name: Per-entity colours
variants.how: Pass `classNameMap={{ Arsenal: "stroke-red-500 fill-red-500" }}`.

variants.name: Fixed scale
variants.how: Always set `min` and `max` so shapes stay comparable across renders.

charts.name: RingGauge
charts.summary: Concentric arcs, one per metric, each filled to its own target — the Apple Watch activity rings pattern.

encodings.description: Key naming each metric.
Key holding the achieved value for each metric.
Key holding each metric’s own target; the ring fills to data ÷ target.
Key holding an error or shortfall value drawn on the ring.

rowCount.note: One ring per row; inner rings get short quickly past ~6.

useWhen: Several metrics each have their own target and should read as a single glanceable unit
Completion against goal is the message rather than absolute values
The set of metrics is stable and small, so ring order can be learned
avoidWhen: Metrics share one scale and their shape should be compared — use RadarChart
There is only one metric — use BulletChart or LinearGauge
Absolute values must be compared across metrics — arc lengths at different radii are not comparable; use ColumnChart
Metrics have no target, only a raw value — use PizzaChart

alternatives.name: BulletChart
alternatives.when: a single metric, with qualitative bands

alternatives.name: RadarChart
alternatives.when: metrics share one scale and profile shape matters

alternatives.name: PizzaChart
alternatives.when: metrics have a shared maximum rather than individual targets

charts.example:
<RingGauge
  id="activity-rings"
  className="w-full h-64"
  data={metrics}
  labelKey="name"
  dataKey="score"
  targetKey="target"
/>

variants.name: Per-ring colours
variants.how: Put a `className` field on each row of `data`.

variants.name: Label placement
variants.how: Set `labels={{ position: "bottom" }}`.

variants.name: Arc geometry
variants.how: Tune `startAngle`, `endAngle`, `cornerRadius`, `minRadius` and `padding.arc`.

charts.name: SpeedometerChart
charts.summary: A dial with a needle showing one value against a scale that can be split into coloured regions.

encodings.description: The value the needle points to. The scale runs 0 to the largest `regions` limit, or 0 to 1 when no regions are given.
`{ text, className }` naming the metric under the dial.
Bands of the arc as `{ limit, className }`; the largest limit also sets the top of the scale.

useWhen: The audience expects a dial metaphor, e.g. an operational or health readout
The scale divides into qualitative bands — good, warning, critical — that should be visible at a glance
One value stands alone on a card and the layout has room for a wide mark
avoidWhen: Space is tight or several gauges will be stacked — use LinearGauge or BulletChart, which pack far denser
Precise reading matters — needle angle is read less accurately than a bar length
Several metrics need comparing — use RingGauge or RadarChart
The trend over time is the real question — use LineChart

alternatives.name: BulletChart
alternatives.when: the same information is needed in a fraction of the space

alternatives.name: LinearGauge
alternatives.when: a plain value on a scale, no bands

alternatives.name: RingGauge
alternatives.when: several metrics each against their own target

charts.example:
<SpeedometerChart
  id="coverage"
  className="w-full h-48"
  data={0.7}
  label={{ text: 'Coverage' }}
/>

variants.name: Coloured regions
variants.how: Pass `regions={[{ limit: 50, className: "fill-red-500" }, { limit: 100, className: "fill-green-500" }]}`; the largest limit becomes the scale maximum.

variants.name: Axis ticks
variants.how: Set `axisTicks={10}` to print values around the arc.

variants.name: Needle length
variants.how: Set `needleRadius` to change how far the needle reaches.

charts.name: Network
charts.summary: Draws nodes and the edges between them, laid out by force simulation or pinned to x/y scales.

encodings.description: Array of node records. Passed separately from `data`.
Array of edge records referencing nodes by id.
Field on each node holding its unique id; edges reference this value.
Field on each edge holding the source node id.
Field on each edge holding the target node id.

rowCount.note: Nodes. Large graphs need filtering or aggregation first.

useWhen: The relationships between entities are the subject, not the entities’ values
Clusters, hubs or isolated nodes should emerge from the layout
Nodes should be positioned by real measures rather than the simulation — set `nodeDef.x` and `nodeDef.y`
The graph is small enough to be explored interactively — enable `dragging` and `zooming`
avoidWhen: The relationships are strictly hierarchical — a tree layout communicates depth better than a force graph
The data has no explicit edges; a network cannot be inferred from records alone
Node values are the real question — use BarChart or ScatterPlot
The graph is dense enough to become a hairball — aggregate or filter first

alternatives.name: ScatterPlot
alternatives.when: entities have two measures and no meaningful links

alternatives.name: WaffleChart
alternatives.when: the relationships form a matrix better read as a heatmap

charts.example:
<Network
  id="team-graph"
  className="w-full h-96"
  nodes={nodes}
  edges={edges}
  nodeDef={{ idKey: 'name' }}
  edgeDef={{ sourceKey: 'from', targetKey: 'to' }}
/>

variants.name: Fixed positions
variants.how: Set `nodeDef.x` and `nodeDef.y` to place nodes on real scales instead of by simulation.

variants.name: Dragging
variants.how: Set `dragging={{ enabled: true, snapToNewPosition: true }}` to let nodes be repositioned and pinned.

variants.name: Encoding
variants.how: Use `nodeDef.size`, `nodeDef.shape` and `nodeDef.classNameKey` with `classNameMap` to encode node attributes.

variants.name: Curved edges
variants.how: Set `edgeDef.curve` and size edges with `edgeDef.size`.
